soundness, provability, Fiat--Shamir, parallel repetition, OR-composition,
abelian group homomorphism.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The question}

A zero-knowledge proof lets a prover convince a verifier that a statement is
true without revealing \emph{why}. The classical instances concern arithmetic
secrets: a discrete logarithm, a graph colouring, a Hamiltonian cycle. This
paper takes the idea to its reflexive limit and asks about mathematics itself:
can one convince a verifier that a theorem $T$ is provable in a fixed formal
system without leaking anything about the proof? A referee wants assurance that
a submitted argument closes; an author may wish to establish priority without
publishing; an automated agent may wish to certify that a search terminated
successfully without exposing the certificate. In each case, ``I hold a proof''
and ``here is the proof'' are very different transmissions, and the gap between
them is exactly the subject of zero knowledge.

\subsection{What is true, what is folklore, what is impossible}

The literature mixes claims that are true in a computational model with claims
that are false in an information-theoretic one, and offers intuitive
explanations of privacy that turn out to be non-explanations. This paper
separates the three: what the protocol really gives (exact simulability, exact
view cardinality, exact soundness error); what is folklore and false (that
privacy requires witness ambiguity, \S\ref{sec:folklore}; that hashing away the
interaction preserves soundness, \S\ref{sec:fs}); and what the protocol cannot
give (any mathematical content not installed by the encoding,
\S\ref{sec:vacuity}).

\subsection{Model}

The adversary is computationally unbounded throughout. Distributional claims are
equalities of multisets over finite index sets, not computational
indistinguishability; soundness claims are cardinality statements about sets of
challenges, not success probabilities under hardness assumptions. This is the
strongest setting for positive results and the harshest for negative ones.

\section{The affine \texorpdfstring{$\Sigma$}{Sigma}-protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}

\begin{definition}[Statement]
Let $G, H$ be abelian groups. A \emph{statement} is a pair $s = (f, T)$ with
$f : G \to H$ a group homomorphism and $T \in H$, read as the assertion
$\exists w \in G,\ f(w) = T$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Witness]
$w \in G$ is a \emph{witness} for $s = (f,T)$ if $f(w) = T$. We write
$W(s) = \{w : f(w) = T\}$ and call $s$ \emph{true} if $W(s) \ne \varnothing$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Challenge selector]
For a bit $c \in \{0,1\}$ and $x$ in an abelian group set
$\chi(c,x) = 0$ if $c = 0$ and $\chi(c,x) = x$ if $c = 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Transcript, acceptance]
A \emph{transcript} is a triple $t = (a,c,z) \in H \times \{0,1\} \times G$
(commitment, challenge, response). It is \emph{accepted} for $s = (f,T)$ if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:verify}
  f(z) = a + \chi(c, T).
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Honest prover and simulator]
For a witness $w$, tape $r \in G$, challenge $c$,
\[
  \Real_s(w,r,c) = \bigl(f(r),\, c,\, r + \chi(c,w)\bigr),
  \qquad
  \Sim_s(z,c) = \bigl(f(z) - \chi(c,T),\, c,\, z\bigr).
\]
The protocol: the prover samples $r$ uniformly and sends $f(r)$; the verifier
samples $c$ uniformly and sends it; the prover sends $r + \chi(c,w)$; the
verifier checks \eqref{eq:verify}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness]\label{thm:complete}
If $f(w) = T$ then $\Real_s(w,r,c)$ is accepted for all $r$ and $c$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $c = 0$: $f(r) = f(r) + 0$. For $c = 1$:
$f(r+w) = f(r) + f(w) = f(r) + T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Simulator validity]\label{thm:simvalid}
$\Sim_s(z,c)$ is accepted for every $z$ and $c$, with no hypothesis on $s$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Equation \eqref{eq:verify} reads $f(z) = (f(z) - \chi(c,T)) + \chi(c,T)$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:simvalid} contains the seed of every negative result below:
acceptance of a \emph{single} transcript is a triviality available to anyone.
All conviction must come from answering \emph{several} challenges.

\begin{theorem}[Special soundness / extraction]\label{thm:extract}
If $(a,0,z_0)$ and $(a,1,z_1)$ are both accepted for $s = (f,T)$, then
$z_1 - z_0$ is a witness for $s$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Acceptance gives $f(z_0) = a$ and $f(z_1) = a + T$; subtract and use additivity:
$f(z_1 - z_0) = T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect zero knowledge]\label{thm:pzk}
Let $G$ be finite, $w$ a witness for $s$, $c$ a challenge. Then as multisets
indexed by $G$,
\[
  \{\!\{\Real_s(w,r,c) : r \in G\}\!\}
  = \{\!\{\Sim_s(z,c) : z \in G\}\!\}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The translation $\tau(r) = r + \chi(c,w)$ is a bijection of $G$. It suffices to
prove $\Real_s(w,r,c) = \Sim_s(\tau(r), c)$ pointwise, since re-indexing a
multiset along a bijection does not change it. Challenge and response agree by
definition; for the commitment we need $f(r + \chi(c,w)) - \chi(c,T) = f(r)$,
which for $c = 0$ is trivial and for $c = 1$ reads $f(r) + f(w) - T = f(r)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Witness indistinguishability]\label{cor:wi}
Two witnesses of the same statement generate identical transcript multisets; the
verifier's view is a function of the public statement alone.
\end{corollary}

\section{Geometry and entropy of the verifier's view}
\label{sec:entropy}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity]\label{thm:inj}
For fixed $s, w, c$ the map $r \mapsto \Real_s(w,r,c)$ is injective; for fixed
$s, c$ the map $z \mapsto \Sim_s(z,c)$ is injective.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Equal transcripts have equal responses, so $r_1 + \chi(c,w) = r_2 + \chi(c,w)$
and cancellation gives $r_1 = r_2$. For the simulator the response \emph{is}
$z$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Uniformity]\label{cor:uniform}
Every transcript occurs at most once in the honest execution: the verifier's
view is uniform on its support.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Support characterisation]\label{thm:support}
If $w$ is a witness for $s$ then
$\{\Real_s(w,r,c) : r \in G\}
 = \{t : t \text{ has challenge } c \text{ and is accepted}\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$(\subseteq)$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}. Conversely let $t = (a,c,z)$ be
accepted and set $r := z - \chi(c,w)$; then $r + \chi(c,w) = z$ and $f(r) = a$
(for $c = 1$: $f(z-w) = (a+T) - T = a$), so $t = \Real_s(w,r,c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Geometry of acceptance]\label{thm:geom}
For \emph{every} statement $s = (f,T)$, true or false, and every challenge $c$,
\[
  \{t : t \text{ has challenge } c \text{ and is accepted}\}
  = \{\Sim_s(z,c) : z \in G\}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$(\supseteq)$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:simvalid}. Conversely, if $(a,c,z)$ is
accepted then \eqref{eq:verify} gives $a = f(z) - \chi(c,T)$, i.e.\ the
transcript is literally $\Sim_s(z,c)$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:geom} is the structural heart of the privacy analysis: the
accepting set is derived from the verification equation alone. The designer has
no freedom; the affine form of \eqref{eq:verify} forces the answer.

\begin{theorem}[View size]\label{thm:viewsize}
Let $G$ be finite. For every statement $s$ and every challenge $c$ the accepting
set with challenge $c$ has exactly $|G|$ elements; the verifier's view is
uniform on it and carries exactly $\log_2 |G|$ bits of Shannon entropy.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:geom} the set is the image of $G$ under an injective map
(Theorem~\ref{thm:inj}), hence of size $|G|$; uniformity is
Corollary~\ref{cor:uniform}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Challenge independence]
Both accepting sets, for $c = 0$ and $c = 1$, have $|G|$ elements: the challenge
bit reveals nothing about the statement.
\end{corollary}

The \emph{quantity} of information reaching the verifier is a constant of the
group: independent of the target, of the truth of the statement, and of the
witness. Every bit originates in the prover's tape; none in the secret.

\section{The witness set is a kernel coset}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:kercoset}
If $w_1, w_2 \in W(s)$ then $w_1 - w_2 \in \ker f$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$f(w_1 - w_2) = T - T = 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Coset structure]\label{thm:coset}
If $w_0 \in W(s)$ then $W(s) = w_0 + \ker f$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $w \in W(s)$ then $w - w_0 \in \ker f$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:kercoset};
conversely $f(w_0 + k) = T + 0 = T$ for $k \in \ker f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Witness count]\label{cor:count}
If $s$ is true then $|W(s)| = |\ker f|$; extraction determines the witness only
modulo $\ker f$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Privacy does not come from witness ambiguity}
\label{sec:folklore}

\begin{theorem}[Unique witness]\label{thm:unique}
If $f$ is injective and $s$ is true then $|W(s)| = 1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Injectivity of a group homomorphism is equivalent to $\ker f = 0$; apply
Corollary~\ref{cor:count}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect zero knowledge with a unique witness]\label{thm:uniquezk}
Let $G$ be finite, $f$ injective, $w$ the unique witness of $s$. Then
$|W(s)| = 1$ and, for each challenge $c$, the honest view equals the simulated
view as a multiset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:unique} and~\ref{thm:pzk}; the latter used only that
$r \mapsto r + \chi(c,w)$ is a bijection and that $f(w) = T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
A widespread informal account holds that a $\Sigma$-protocol hides the witness
because many witnesses are consistent with the public statement.
Theorem~\ref{thm:uniquezk} refutes this in the sharpest form: with a unique
witness there is nothing to be ambiguous about, and the view is still exactly
the simulator's. Witness ambiguity (Corollary~\ref{cor:count}) governs the
resolution of \emph{extraction}; translation symmetry of the tape space governs
\emph{privacy}.
\end{remark}

\section{Amplification and the provability compiler}

\subsection{Parallel repetition}

\begin{definition}[Committed parallel prover]
For $n \ge 1$, a \emph{committed prover} is a pair $P = (a, \rho)$ with
$a \in H^n$ fixed in advance and $\rho : \{0,1\}^n \to G^n$ arbitrary. The
parallel verifier accepts $c \in \{0,1\}^n$ if $f(\rho(c)_i) = a_i + \chi(c_i,T)$
for all $i$. The \emph{cheat set} $\Ch(P)$ is the set of accepted vectors.
\end{definition}

The response function may depend on the whole challenge vector and is subject to
no computational restriction.

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity]\label{thm:rigid}
If $s$ is false then $|\Ch(P)| \le 1$ for every committed prover.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Two distinct accepted vectors differ in some coordinate $i$; at the single
commitment $a_i$ the prover has answered both challenge values, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:extract} produces a witness --- a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness error]\label{thm:soundness}
If $s$ is false then $|\Ch(P)| / 2^{n} \le (1/2)^n$ for every committed prover.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Full completeness]\label{thm:fullcomplete}
The honest parallel prover built from a witness $w$ and tapes $r \in G^n$,
namely $a_i = f(r_i)$ and $\rho(c)_i = r_i + \chi(c_i,w)$, has
$\Ch(P) = \{0,1\}^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Amplified dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
For every committed prover, either $|\Ch(P)| \le 1$, or $s$ has a witness and
the honest prover built from it answers all $2^n$ challenge vectors for every
choice of tapes. There is no intermediate regime.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Compiling a formal system}

\begin{definition}[Provability compilation]\label{def:compile}
Let $\mathsf{Thm}$ be a set of theorem statements, $\mathsf{Prf}$ a set of
candidate proof objects and $\Chk \subseteq \mathsf{Thm}\times\mathsf{Prf}$ a
checking relation. A \emph{provability compilation} of $T_0$ consists of a
public statement $s = (f,\mathrm{target})$ and an encoding
$E : \mathsf{Prf} \to G$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item $\Chk(T_0,p) \implies f(E(p)) = \mathrm{target}$;
  \item $\exists w,\ f(w) = \mathrm{target} \implies \exists p,\ \Chk(T_0,p)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Provability equivalence]\label{thm:equiv}
$T_0$ is provable if and only if the compiled statement $s$ is true.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Conviction]\label{thm:conviction}
If some commitment $a$ admits accepted responses $z_0, z_1$ to both challenges,
then $T_0$ is provable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:extract} yields the witness $z_1 - z_0$; axiom (ii) of
Definition~\ref{def:compile} converts it into a checking proof.
\end{proof}

The extracted object is a group element, not a proof: the verifier learns the
\emph{existence} of a proof, mediated by the faithfulness of the encoding.

\begin{theorem}[Zero-knowledge provability transfer]\label{thm:transfer}
Let $G$ be finite and fix a provability compilation of $T_0$. Then:
(1) any two checking proofs $p_1, p_2$ of $T_0$ induce identical verifier views
for each challenge; (2) that common view equals the output of the simulator,
which sees only the public statement; (3) any double answer at one commitment
certifies that $T_0$ is provable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(2) follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:pzk} applied to the witness $E(p)$; (1) from
(2) applied twice; (3) is Theorem~\ref{thm:conviction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unprovability is exponentially hard to fake]\label{thm:unprov}
If $T_0$ is unprovable then every committed prover answers at most a $2^{-n}$
fraction of the $2^n$ challenge vectors.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No double answer]\label{thm:nodouble}
If $T_0$ is unprovable, there are no $a, z_0, z_1$ with $(a,0,z_0)$ and
$(a,1,z_1)$ both accepted: the extraction event never occurs, rather than
occurring and extracting garbage.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Provability gap synthesis]\label{thm:gap}
Fix a provability compilation of $T_0$, a round count $n$ and a challenge $c$.
All of the following hold simultaneously.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item If $T_0$ is unprovable, every committed prover has
        $|\Ch(P)|/2^n \le (1/2)^n$.
  \item If $p$ is a checking proof of $T_0$, the honest prover built from $E(p)$
        answers all $2^n$ challenge vectors for every choice of tapes, and its
        view equals the simulator's output.
  \item Regardless of provability, the accepting set with challenge $c$ has
        exactly $|G|$ elements.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\subsection{A boundary: compiler vacuity}
\label{sec:vacuity}

\begin{theorem}[Vacuity of the zero compilation]\label{thm:vacuous}
Take $f = 0 : G \to H$ with target $0$, any encoding $E$, and any theorem $T_0$
possessing at least one checking proof. Then every $w \in G$ is a witness, both
axioms of Definition~\ref{def:compile} hold trivially, extraction always
succeeds, and the protocol certifies nothing beyond what the encoding already
assumed.
\end{theorem}

This is a delimitation of scope rather than a defect. The protocol transports
the assertion ``the compiled statement is true'' with perfect privacy and error
$2^{-n}$; that this assertion \emph{means} ``$T_0$ is provable'' is exactly the
content of Definition~\ref{def:compile}, which must be established outside the
protocol. Cryptography cannot manufacture mathematical content; it can only move
existing content while hiding its shape.

\section{The Fiat--Shamir inversion}
\label{sec:fs}

\begin{definition}
Let $\Hash : H \to \{0,1\}$ be arbitrary. The pair $(a,z)$ is a
\emph{non-interactive proof} for $s$ if $(a, \Hash(a), z)$ is accepted, i.e.
$f(z) = a + \chi(\Hash(a),T)$. The hash is \emph{forgery-free} for $s$ if no
non-interactive proof exists.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-point description]\label{thm:fixedpoint}
A non-interactive proof exists iff there are $z \in G$ and $c \in \{0,1\}$ with
$\Hash\bigl(f(z) - \chi(c,T)\bigr) = c$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Given $(a,z)$ accepted, put $c = \Hash(a)$; the verification equation gives
$a = f(z) - \chi(c,T)$. Conversely, given such $z$ and $c$, put
$a := f(z) - \chi(c,T)$; then $\Hash(a) = c$ and $a + \chi(c,T) = f(z)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of forgery-freeness]\label{thm:ffiff}
$\Hash$ is forgery-free for $s = (f,T)$ iff $\Hash(f(z)) = 1$ for all $z$ and
$\Hash(f(z) - T) = 0$ for all $z$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Negate the fixed-point condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:fixedpoint} at $c = 0$ and
at $c = 1$ respectively.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Every hash is forgeable on true statements]\label{thm:allforge}
If $s$ has a witness $w$, then for \emph{every} $\Hash$ an accepted
non-interactive proof exists.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $\Hash(0) = 0$ take $z = 0$, $c = 0$: then $f(z) - \chi(0,T) = 0$. If
$\Hash(0) = 1$ take $z = w$, $c = 1$: then $f(w) - T = 0$. In both cases
Theorem~\ref{thm:fixedpoint} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forgery-freeness on false statements]\label{thm:imagehash}
If $s$ has no witness, the image colouring $\Hash^{\ast}(a) = 1$ iff
$a \in \im f$ is forgery-free.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:ffiff} is immediate. If
$f(z) - T = f(y)$ for some $y$, then $f(z-y) = T$, a witness --- impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Fiat--Shamir inversion]\label{thm:fsinv}
A forgery-free hash exists for a statement if and only if that statement is
\emph{false}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Necessity of interaction]\label{thm:interaction}
For every statement and every $n$: if the statement is false, every committed
prover in the $n$-round interactive protocol answers at most a $2^{-n}$ fraction
of the challenge vectors; if it is true, every hash function whatsoever admits
an accepted non-interactive proof.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
In the information-theoretic model, unconditional non-interactive soundness
holds precisely when the statement one wishes to prove is untrue --- the exact
opposite of what a proof system requires. Practical deployments are not thereby
refuted: their security is a \emph{computational} statement, asserting that
although forgeries exist in abundance, none can be found in feasible time.
Theorem~\ref{thm:fsinv} delimits what any such argument must be: it cannot be
information-theoretic, and it cannot be improved by cleverness in the choice of
hash.
\end{remark}

\section{Large challenge spaces: \texorpdfstring{$\FF_q$}{Fq}-linear statements}

Let $q$ be prime and $\FF_q = \mathbb{Z}/q$.

\begin{definition}
A \emph{linear statement} over $\FF_q$-vector spaces $V, W$ is $s = (f,T)$ with
$f : V \to W$ linear and $T \in W$; a witness satisfies $f(w) = T$. A transcript
$(a,c,z) \in W \times \FF_q \times V$ is accepted iff $f(z) = a + cT$, with
$\Real_s(w,r,c) = (f(r), c, r + cw)$ and $\Sim_s(z,c) = (f(z) - cT, c, z)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect zero knowledge]\label{thm:linpzk}
For finite $V$, a witness $w$ and $c \in \FF_q$, the honest and simulated views
coincide as multisets.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$r \mapsto r + cw$ is a bijection of $V$ and
$\Real_s(w,r,c) = \Sim_s(r + cw, c)$, since
$f(r + cw) - cT = f(r) + cf(w) - cT = f(r)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Linear special soundness]\label{thm:linextract}
Let $c \ne c'$ in $\FF_q$ and suppose $(a,c,z)$ and $(a,c',z')$ are both
accepted. Then $w := (c-c')^{-1}(z - z')$ is a witness.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Subtracting the verification equations gives $f(z - z') = (c - c')T$; since
$\FF_q$ is a field and $c \ne c'$, the scalar $c - c'$ is invertible, and
$f\bigl((c-c')^{-1}(z-z')\bigr) = T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness $q^{-n}$]\label{thm:linsound}
If $s$ has no witness, a committed prover in the $n$-fold parallel repetition
answers at most one of the $q^n$ challenge vectors, an accepting fraction of at
most $(1/q)^n$. If $s$ has a witness, the honest prover answers all $q^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The Boolean protocol is the case $q = 2$]\label{thm:q2}
Over an $\FF_2$-vector space, $\chi(c,w) = \bar{c}\,w$ where $\bar c \in \FF_2$
is the image of the bit $c$.
\end{theorem}

Larger $q$ buys soundness at the cost of a challenge of $\log_2 q$ bits; the
view size remains $|V|$ regardless.

\section{OR-composition: hiding which theorem}

\begin{definition}
An \emph{OR-transcript} is a tuple $(a_1,a_2,c_1,c_2,z_1,z_2)$, accepted for the
challenge $c$ if $c_1 \oplus c_2 = c$ and $(a_i,c_i,z_i)$ is accepted for $s_i$,
$i = 1,2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The two strategies]
Randomness is $(r,z,d) \in G \times G \times \{0,1\}$. The \emph{left strategy},
for a prover holding a witness $w_1$ of $s_1$, outputs
\[
  \bigl(f_1(r),\; f_2(z) - \chi(d,T_2),\; c \oplus d,\; d,\;
        r + \chi(c \oplus d, w_1),\; z\bigr),
\]
and the \emph{right strategy}, for a prover holding a witness $w_2$ of $s_2$,
outputs
\[
  \bigl(f_1(z) - \chi(d,T_1),\; f_2(r),\; d,\; c \oplus d,\; z,\;
        r + \chi(c \oplus d, w_2)\bigr).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness]\label{thm:orcomplete}
Each strategy produces an accepted OR-transcript for every challenge and every
value of its randomness: the honest branch by Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}, the
simulated branch by Theorem~\ref{thm:simvalid}, and the XOR constraint by
construction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Which-theorem hiding]\label{thm:orhiding}
Let $G$ be finite and let $w_1, w_2$ be witnesses for $s_1, s_2$. For every
challenge $c$, the left and right strategies generate exactly the same multiset
of OR-transcripts as the randomness ranges over $G\times G\times\{0,1\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The reparametrisation
$\sigma(r,z,d) = \bigl(z - \chi(d,w_2),\, r + \chi(c\oplus d, w_1),\,
c \oplus d\bigr)$
is a bijection of $G\times G\times\{0,1\}$, with inverse
$(r,z,e) \mapsto \bigl(z - \chi(e,w_1),\, r + \chi(c\oplus e, w_2),\,
c\oplus e\bigr)$; the bit component is the involution $d \mapsto c\oplus d$ and
the group components are translations composed with a swap. A componentwise
computation using $f_1(w_1) = T_1$ and $f_2(w_2) = T_2$ shows that the left
strategy at $(r,z,d)$ equals the right strategy at $\sigma(r,z,d)$. Re-indexing
a multiset along a bijection leaves it unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Disjunctive soundness]\label{thm:orsound}
If two OR-transcripts are accepted for challenges $c \ne c'$ and share both
commitments, then $s_1$ or $s_2$ has a witness.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $c_1 \oplus c_2 \ne c_1' \oplus c_2'$, the sub-challenges differ in at
least one branch; at that branch's shared commitment both challenge values have
been answered, and Theorem~\ref{thm:extract} extracts a witness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[OR-provability transfer]\label{thm:ortransfer}
For two provability compilations of theorems $T_1, T_2$ over the same groups,
with checking proofs $p_1$ and $p_2$: two accepted OR-conversations with the
same commitments and different challenges certify that at least one of $T_1,
T_2$ is provable, while the view of the prover using the proof of $T_1$ equals
the view of the prover using the proof of $T_2$. Conviction about the
disjunction is transferred; the identity of the provable disjunct is not.
\end{theorem}

\section{Fully explicit instances}

\subsection{The Boolean protocol over \texorpdfstring{$\mathbb{Z}/12$}{Z/12}}

Let $G = H = \mathbb{Z}/12$ and $f(x) = 4x$.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item True statement $s^{+} = (f, 8)$: witnesses $\{2,5,8,11\}$, so
        $|W(s^+)| = 4$; and $\ker f = \{0,3,6,9\}$ also has $4$ elements,
        confirming Corollary~\ref{cor:count}.
  \item False statement $s^{-} = (f,1)$: $\im f = \{0,4,8\} \not\ni 1$.
  \item Extraction: at commitment $a = 4r$ the responses $z_0 = r$ and
        $z_1 = r+2$ are accepted for $s^{+}$, and $z_1 - z_0 = 2$ is a witness.
  \item Soundness: over $n = 10$ rounds a committed prover answers at most a
        $1/1024$ fraction of the $1024$ challenge vectors for $s^{-}$.
  \item Zero knowledge: the witnesses $2$ and $5$ generate identical transcript
        multisets for either challenge.
  \item View size: for either challenge, both $s^{+}$ and $s^{-}$ admit exactly
        $12$ accepting transcripts.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{The linear protocol over \texorpdfstring{$\FF_5$}{F5}}

Let $V = W = \FF_5$.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item True statement $f = \mathrm{id}$, $T = 3$: the witness $w = 3$ is
        unique, a live instance of Theorem~\ref{thm:uniquezk}.
  \item False statement $f = 0$, $T = 1$: no witness.
  \item Extraction: at $c = 1$, $c' = 4$ the honest responses are $r + 3$ and
        $r + 2$, and $(1-4)^{-1}\cdot 1 = 3$ recovers the witness.
  \item Soundness: over $n = 4$ rounds a committed prover answers at most a
        $1/625$ fraction of the $625$ challenge vectors for the false statement.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion and open problems}

\subsection{What the theory delivers}

By Theorem~\ref{thm:gap}, for a faithfully compiled theorem the interactive
protocol transmits exactly one bit --- ``the theorem is provable'' --- to within
error $2^{-n}$ (or $q^{-n}$), while the verifier's entire view is a uniform
sample from a set of size $|G|$ that is the \emph{same} set whether the theorem
is provable or not. Applications suggested by the framework include priority
without publication, referee-side assurance of closure without disclosure of a
proprietary certificate, delegation and audit of searches whose outputs are
encodable as witnesses of public linear conditions, and disjunctive claims via
Theorem~\ref{thm:ortransfer}.

\subsection{What it does not deliver}

Three limitations, all proved above: the encoding is the load-bearing assumption
(Theorem~\ref{thm:vacuous}); interaction cannot be removed for free
(Theorem~\ref{thm:fsinv}); and privacy is not measured by witness count
(Theorem~\ref{thm:uniquezk}).

\subsection{Conjectures}

\begin{conjecture}[Entropy rigidity]
For any three-move protocol over a finite abelian group whose verification
predicate is affine in the response, the Shannon entropy of the verifier's view
equals $\log_2|G|$ exactly, with no slack; and perfect zero knowledge holds if
and only if the accepting set is a torsor under the tape group.
\end{conjecture}

The evidence is Theorem~\ref{thm:geom}, which derives the accepting set from the
verification equation alone: entropy is forced by the affine form and cannot be
tuned by the designer. Only the passage from cardinalities to entropies remains.

\begin{conjecture}[Knowledge error equals the kernel index]
For a linear map $f : V \to W$ over $\FF_q$, the probabilistic extractor of the
$n$-round protocol has knowledge error exactly $q^{-n}$ and recovers the witness
precisely modulo $\ker f$; the privacy margin and the knowledge error are two
readings of the same subgroup index.
\end{conjecture}

The evidence is Corollary~\ref{cor:count}, identifying the witness set with a
coset of $\ker f$, together with Theorem~\ref{thm:linsound}.

\subsection{Further directions}

Upgrade Theorem~\ref{thm:viewsize} from cardinalities to Shannon entropies;
characterise the verification predicates for which Theorem~\ref{thm:geom}
survives (affinity in the response is sufficient --- is a weaker torsor
condition necessary?); extend to non-abelian groups and to modules over rings
where $c - c'$ need not be invertible; construct explicit faithful compilations
of concrete proof calculi so that Definition~\ref{def:compile} becomes a theorem
about a real checker; and identify the minimal computational assumption
circumventing Theorem~\ref{thm:fsinv}.

\section{Conclusion}

The affine $\Sigma$-protocol supports an unusually complete information-theoretic
analysis. Its privacy is exact and its source identified: the translation
symmetry of the tape group, not the ambiguity of the secret. Its soundness is
not merely small but rigid --- at most one accepted challenge vector out of
$2^n$ (or $q^n$) without a witness, all of them with one, and nothing in
between. Its conviction transfers to statements about formal provability, giving
a precise sense in which one can convince a sceptic that a theorem has a proof
while transmitting no information about which proof one holds. The negative
results are equally precise, and they are the reason to trust the positive ones:
removing the interaction destroys unconditional soundness, and a degenerate
encoding renders the apparatus vacuous. The protocol is a perfect courier of
conviction, and never a source of it.

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Types
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Elem = int                       # element of Z/m, represented as 0..m-1
Transcript = Tuple[int, int, int]  # (commitment, challenge, response)
OrTranscript = Tuple[int, int, int, int, int, int]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The Boolean affine protocol over a cyclic group
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


class AffineStatement:
    """The public statement 'exists w in Z/m with k*w = target'.

    The homomorphism is f(x) = k*x on Z/m; the challenge selector is
    chi(c, x) = x if c == 1 else 0.
    """

    def __init__(self, modulus: int, k: int, target: int) -> None:
        self.m: int = modulus
        self.k: int = k % modulus
        self.target: int = target % modulus

    # -- basic maps ---------------------------------------------------------

    def f(self, x: Elem) -> Elem:
        return (self.k * x) % self.m

    def chi(self, c: int, x: Elem) -> Elem:
        return x % self.m if c == 1 else 0

    def elements(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return list(range(self.m))

    # -- witnesses ----------------------------------------------------------

    def witnesses(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return [w for w in self.elements() if self.f(w) == self.target]

    def kernel(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return [x for x in self.elements() if self.f(x) == 0]

    def image(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return sorted({self.f(x) for x in self.elements()})

    # -- protocol -----------------------------------------------------------

    def accepts(self, t: Transcript) -> bool:
        a, c, z = t
        return self.f(z) == (a + self.chi(c, self.target)) % self.m

    def real(self, w: Elem, r: Elem, c: int) -> Transcript:
        return (self.f(r), c, (r + self.chi(c, w)) % self.m)

    def sim(self, z: Elem, c: int) -> Transcript:
        return ((self.f(z) - self.chi(c, self.target)) % self.m, c, z)

    def real_view(self, w: Elem, c: int) -> Counter:
        return Counter(self.real(w, r, c) for r in self.elements())

    def sim_view(self, c: int) -> Counter:
        return Counter(self.sim(z, c) for z in self.elements())

    def accepting_set(self, c: int) -> List[Transcript]:
        return [
            (a, c, z)
            for a in self.elements()
            for z in self.elements()
            if self.accepts((a, c, z))
        ]

    @staticmethod
    def extract(z_false: Elem, z_true: Elem, modulus: int) -> Elem:
        """Special soundness: two answers at one commitment give a witness."""
        return (z_true - z_false) % modulus


def demo_boolean_protocol() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. THE BOOLEAN AFFINE PROTOCOL OVER Z/12 WITH f(x) = 4x")
    print("=" * 74)

    true_stmt = AffineStatement(12, 4, 8)    # 4w = 8   -- solvable
    false_stmt = AffineStatement(12, 4, 1)   # 4w = 1   -- unsolvable

          f"{len(true_stmt.witnesses())} = {len(true_stmt.kernel())}  "
          f"{len(true_stmt.witnesses()) == len(true_stmt.kernel())}")
    print(f"witnesses of 4w = 1   : {false_stmt.witnesses()}  (statement false)")

    # completeness
    ok = all(
        true_stmt.accepts(true_stmt.real(w, r, c))

    print("\nperfect zero knowledge (exact multiset identities):")
    for c in (0, 1):

    same = true_stmt.real_view(2, 1) == true_stmt.real_view(5, 1)
    print(f"\nwitnesses 2 and 5 give identical views          : {same}")

    print("\nview size (Theorem: |accepting set| = |G| always):")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Parallel repetition and the cheat set
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cheat_set(
    stmt: AffineStatement,
    commitments: Sequence[int],
    respond: Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], Tuple[int, ...]],
) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Challenge vectors an already-committed prover can answer."""
    n = len(commitments)
    good: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for c in product((0, 1), repeat=n):
        z = respond(c)
        if all(stmt.accepts((commitments[i], c[i], z[i])) for i in range(n)):
            good.append(c)
    return good


def best_cheating_prover(
    stmt: AffineStatement, commitments: Sequence[int]
) -> Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """The optimal (unbounded) adversary: for each challenge vector, answer
    each round with any response that satisfies the verification equation,
    if one exists."""
    n = len(commitments)

    def respond(c: Tuple[int, ...]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
        out: List[int] = []
        for i in range(n):
            found = 0
            for z in stmt.elements():
                if stmt.accepts((commitments[i], c[i], z)):
                    found = z
                    break
            out.append(found)
        return tuple(out)

    return respond


def demo_parallel_repetition() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. PARALLEL REPETITION: EXHAUSTIVE CHEAT-SET ENUMERATION")
    print("=" * 74)

    false_stmt = AffineStatement(12, 4, 1)
    true_stmt = AffineStatement(12, 4, 8)

    print("false statement 4w = 1: optimal unbounded prover, all commitment")
    print("vectors enumerated; |cheat set| out of 2^n.\n")
    for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        worst = 0
        for commitments in product(range(12), repeat=n):
            cs = cheat_set(false_stmt, commitments, best_cheating_prover(false_stmt, commitments))
            worst = max(worst, len(cs))
        print(f"  n = {n}: max |cheat set| over all commitments = {worst} "
              f"out of {2 ** n}   (bound: 1, fraction <= {1 / 2 ** n:.6f})")

    print("\ntrue statement 4w = 8: honest prover with witness 2, tapes all zero")
    for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        commitments = tuple(true_stmt.f(0) for _ in range(n))

        def honest(c: Tuple[int, ...], n: int = n) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
            return tuple(true_stmt.chi(c[i], 2) for i in range(n))

        cs = cheat_set(true_stmt, commitments, honest)
        print(f"  n = {n}: |cheat set| = {len(cs)} out of {2 ** n}  (all of them)")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The Fiat-Shamir inversion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def forgery_exists(stmt: AffineStatement, hash_fn: Callable[[int], int]) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Return an accepted non-interactive pair (a, z), or None."""
    for z in stmt.elements():
        for c in (0, 1):
            a = (stmt.f(z) - stmt.chi(c, stmt.target)) % stmt.m
            if hash_fn(a) == c:
                return (a, z)
    return None


def all_hashes(m: int) -> Iterable[Callable[[int], int]]:
    """Enumerate every function Z/m -> {0,1}.  Only feasible for tiny m."""
    for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=m):
        yield (lambda a, bits=bits: bits[a % m])


def demo_fiat_shamir() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. THE FIAT-SHAMIR INVERSION")
    print("=" * 74)

    # small group so that all 2^m hash functions can be enumerated
    true_small = AffineStatement(6, 2, 4)    # 2w = 4 mod 6 : witnesses 2, 5
    false_small = AffineStatement(6, 2, 1)   # 2w = 1 mod 6 : none

    print(f"group Z/6, f(x) = 2x; image = {true_small.image()}")
    print(f"true  statement 2w = 4: witnesses {true_small.witnesses()}")
    print(f"false statement 2w = 1: witnesses {false_small.witnesses()}")

    total = 2 ** 6
    forgeable_true = sum(1 for h in all_hashes(6) if forgery_exists(true_small, h))
    forgeable_false = sum(1 for h in all_hashes(6) if forgery_exists(false_small, h))
    print(f"\nhash functions Z/6 -> {{0,1}} enumerated: {total}")
    print(f"  TRUE  statement: hashes admitting a forgery = {forgeable_true} / {total}")
    print(f"  FALSE statement: hashes admitting a forgery = {forgeable_false} / {total}")
    print(f"  => forgery-free hashes exist iff the statement is FALSE: "
          f"{forgeable_true == total and forgeable_false < total}")

    # the canonical forgery-free hash on the false statement
    image = set(false_small.image())
    image_hash: Callable[[int], int] = lambda a: 1 if a % 6 in image else 0
    print(f"\nimage colouring on the false statement is forgery-free : "
          f"{forgery_exists(false_small, image_hash) is None}")
    print(f"image colouring on the true  statement is forgeable     : "
          f"{forgery_exists(true_small, image_hash) is not None}")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The linear protocol over F_q
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


class LinearStatement:
    """f(x) = k*x on F_q (q prime), target T; challenges range over F_q."""

    def __init__(self, q: int, k: int, target: int) -> None:
        self.q: int = q
        self.k: int = k % q
        self.target: int = target % q

    def f(self, x: int) -> int:
        return (self.k * x) % self.q

    def elements(self) -> List[int]:
        return list(range(self.q))

    def witnesses(self) -> List[int]:
        return [w for w in self.elements() if self.f(w) == self.target]

    def accepts(self, a: int, c: int, z: int) -> bool:
        return self.f(z) == (a + c * self.target) % self.q

    def real(self, w: int, r: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return (self.f(r), c, (r + c * w) % self.q)

    def sim(self, z: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return ((self.f(z) - c * self.target) % self.q, c, z)

    def extract(self, c: int, z: int, c2: int, z2: int) -> int:
        """w = (c - c')^{-1} (z - z') in F_q."""
        diff = (c - c2) % self.q
        inv = pow(diff, self.q - 2, self.q)  # Fermat inverse, q prime
        return (inv * (z - z2)) % self.q


def demo_linear() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. LINEAR PROTOCOL OVER F_q: SOUNDNESS q^{-n} AND LINEAR EXTRACTION")
    print("=" * 74)

    q = 5
    id_stmt = LinearStatement(q, 1, 3)     # w = 3, unique witness
    zero_stmt = LinearStatement(q, 0, 1)   # no witness

    print(f"F_5, identity map, target 3 : witnesses {id_stmt.witnesses()}")
    print(f"F_5, zero map,     target 1 : witnesses {zero_stmt.witnesses()}")

    # perfect zero knowledge over every challenge in F_q
    ok = all(
        Counter(id_stmt.real(3, r, c) for r in id_stmt.elements())
        == Counter(id_stmt.sim(z, c) for z in id_stmt.elements())
        for c in range(q)
    )
    print(f"perfect zero knowledge for every challenge in F_5 : {ok}")

    # linear extraction from two distinct challenges
    r = 4
    a = id_stmt.f(r)
    c, c2 = 1, 4
    z = (r + c * 3) % q
    z2 = (r + c2 * 3) % q
    assert id_stmt.accepts(a, c, z) and id_stmt.accepts(a, c2, z2)
    print(f"extraction from challenges {c} and {c2}: "
          f"(c-c')^-1 (z-z') = {id_stmt.extract(c, z, c2, z2)}  (witness is 3)")

    # exhaustive soundness for the false statement
    print("\nfalse statement, optimal unbounded prover, all commitments:")
    for n in (1, 2):
        worst = 0
        for commitments in product(range(q), repeat=n):
            good = 0
            for cs in product(range(q), repeat=n):
                answerable = True
                for i in range(n):
                    if not any(zero_stmt.accepts(commitments[i], cs[i], z)
                               for z in zero_stmt.elements()):
                        answerable = False
                        break
                good += 1 if answerable else 0
            worst = max(worst, good)
        print(f"  n = {n}: max |cheat set| = {worst} out of {q ** n} "
              f"(bound 1, fraction <= {1 / q ** n:.6f})")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. OR-composition
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def or_left(
    s1: AffineStatement, s2: AffineStatement, w1: int, c: int, r: int, z: int, d: int
) -> OrTranscript:
    m = s1.m
    return (
        s1.f(r),
        (s2.f(z) - s2.chi(d, s2.target)) % m,
        c ^ d,
        d,
        (r + s1.chi(c ^ d, w1)) % m,
        z,
    )


def or_right(
    s1: AffineStatement, s2: AffineStatement, w2: int, c: int, r: int, z: int, d: int
) -> OrTranscript:
    m = s1.m
    return (
        (s1.f(z) - s1.chi(d, s1.target)) % m,
        s2.f(r),
        d,
        c ^ d,
        z,
        (r + s2.chi(c ^ d, w2)) % m,
    )


def or_accepts(s1: AffineStatement, s2: AffineStatement, c: int, t: OrTranscript) -> bool:
    a1, a2, c1, c2, z1, z2 = t
    return (c1 ^ c2) == c and s1.accepts((a1, c1, z1)) and s2.accepts((a2, c2, z2))


def demo_or_composition() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. OR-COMPOSITION: WHICH-THEOREM HIDING")
    print("=" * 74)

    s1 = AffineStatement(6, 2, 4)   # witnesses 2, 5
    s2 = AffineStatement(6, 3, 3)   # witnesses 1, 3, 5
    w1, w2 = s1.witnesses()[0], s2.witnesses()[0]
    print(f"s1: 2w = 4 mod 6, witnesses {s1.witnesses()} (using {w1})")
    print(f"s2: 3w = 3 mod 6, witnesses {s2.witnesses()} (using {w2})")

    rand = [(r, z, d) for r in range(6) for z in range(6) for d in (0, 1)]
    for c in (0, 1):
        left = Counter(or_left(s1, s2, w1, c, r, z, d) for (r, z, d) in rand)
        right = Counter(or_right(s1, s2, w2, c, r, z, d) for (r, z, d) in rand)
        complete = all(or_accepts(s1, s2, c, t) for t in left)
        print(f"challenge {c}: left view == right view : {left == right}   "
              f"(all accepted: {complete}, {sum(left.values())} conversations)")

    print("\nThe verifier cannot tell which of the two statements the prover")
    print("is able to prove: the two strategies induce the same distribution.")

    # disjunctive soundness, illustrated
    r, z, d = 1, 2, 0
    t0 = or_left(s1, s2, w1, 0, r, z, d)
    t1 = or_left(s1, s2, w1, 1, r, z, d)
    shares = (t0[0], t0[1]) == (t1[0], t1[1])
    print(f"\ntwo conversations, same commitments {shares}, challenges 0 and 1")
    print(f"  => sub-challenges differ somewhere: "
          f"{(t0[2] != t1[2]) or (t0[3] != t1[3])} => a witness is extractable")

    for p, e in checking_proofs.items():

    print("\n(i) identical views for the two proofs, each challenge:")
    for c in (0, 1):
        v = [stmt.real_view(e, c) for e in checking_proofs.values()]
        print(f"  challenge {c}: views equal = {v[0] == v[1]}, "
              f"equal to simulator = {v[0] == stmt.sim_view(c)}")

    print("\n(ii) conviction: a double answer certifies provability.")
    r = 3
    a = stmt.f(r)
    z0, z1 = r, (r + 2) % 12

    unprov = AffineStatement(12, 4, 1)

    print(f"      witnesses of the compiled statement: {unprov.witnesses()}")

    print("\n(iv) BOUNDARY: with the zero homomorphism every element is a")
    print("     witness, so the compilation certifies nothing at all.")
    vacuous = AffineStatement(12, 0, 0)

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Types
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Elem = int                       # element of Z/m, represented as 0..m-1
Transcript = Tuple[int, int, int]  # (commitment, challenge, response)
OrTranscript = Tuple[int, int, int, int, int, int]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The Boolean affine protocol over a cyclic group
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


class AffineStatement:
    """The public statement 'exists w in Z/m with k*w = target'.

    The homomorphism is f(x) = k*x on Z/m; the challenge selector is
    chi(c, x) = x if c == 1 else 0.
    """

    def __init__(self, modulus: int, k: int, target: int) -> None:
        self.m: int = modulus
        self.k: int = k % modulus
        self.target: int = target % modulus

    # -- basic maps ---------------------------------------------------------

    def f(self, x: Elem) -> Elem:
        return (self.k * x) % self.m

    def chi(self, c: int, x: Elem) -> Elem:
        return x % self.m if c == 1 else 0

    def elements(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return list(range(self.m))

    # -- witnesses ----------------------------------------------------------

    def witnesses(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return [w for w in self.elements() if self.f(w) == self.target]

    def kernel(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return [x for x in self.elements() if self.f(x) == 0]

    def image(self) -> List[Elem]:
        return sorted({self.f(x) for x in self.elements()})

    # -- protocol -----------------------------------------------------------

    def accepts(self, t: Transcript) -> bool:
        a, c, z = t
        return self.f(z) == (a + self.chi(c, self.target)) % self.m

    def real(self, w: Elem, r: Elem, c: int) -> Transcript:
        return (self.f(r), c, (r + self.chi(c, w)) % self.m)

    def sim(self, z: Elem, c: int) -> Transcript:
        return ((self.f(z) - self.chi(c, self.target)) % self.m, c, z)

    def real_view(self, w: Elem, c: int) -> Counter:
        return Counter(self.real(w, r, c) for r in self.elements())

    def sim_view(self, c: int) -> Counter:
        return Counter(self.sim(z, c) for z in self.elements())

    def accepting_set(self, c: int) -> List[Transcript]:
        return [
            (a, c, z)
            for a in self.elements()
            for z in self.elements()
            if self.accepts((a, c, z))
        ]

    @staticmethod
    def extract(z_false: Elem, z_true: Elem, modulus: int) -> Elem:
        """Special soundness: two answers at one commitment give a witness."""
        return (z_true - z_false) % modulus


def demo_boolean_protocol() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. THE BOOLEAN AFFINE PROTOCOL OVER Z/12 WITH f(x) = 4x")
    print("=" * 74)

    false_stmt = AffineStatement(12, 4, 1)   # 4w = 1   -- unsolvable

    print(f"witnesses of 4w = 8   : {true_stmt.witnesses()}")
    print(f"kernel of f           : {true_stmt.kernel()}")
    print(f"|W| = |ker f|         : "
          f"{len(true_stmt.witnesses())} = {len(true_stmt.kernel())}  "
          f"{len(true_stmt.witnesses()) == len(true_stmt.kernel())}")
    print(f"witnesses of 4w = 1   : {false_stmt.witnesses()}  (statement false)")

    # completeness

        true_stmt.accepts(true_stmt.real(w, r, c))
        for w in true_stmt.witnesses()
        for r in true_stmt.elements()
        for c in (0, 1)
    )
    print(f"\ncompleteness (all witnesses, tapes, challenges) : {ok}")

    # simulator validity, for the FALSE statement too
    ok = all(
        false_stmt.accepts(false_stmt.sim(z, c))
        for z in false_stmt.elements()
        for c in (0, 1)
    )
    print(f"simulator valid even for a FALSE statement      : {ok}")

    # extraction
    r = 7
    a = true_stmt.f(r)
    z0, z1 = r, (r + 2) % 12

          f"is a witness: {true_stmt.f(w) == true_stmt.target}")

    # perfect zero knowledge as exact multiset identity
    print("\nperfect zero knowledge (exact multiset identities):")
    for c in (0, 1):
        for w in true_stmt.witnesses():
            same = true_stmt.real_view(w, c) == true_stmt.sim_view(c)
            print(f"  challenge {c}, witness {w:2d}: real view == sim view : {same}")

    # witness indistinguishability
    same = true_stmt.real_view(2, 1) == true_stmt.real_view(5, 1)
    print(f"\nwitnesses 2 and 5 give identical views          : {same}")

    # view size
    print("\nview size (Theorem: |accepting set| = |G| always):")
    for name, st in (("true  4w=8", true_stmt), ("false 4w=1", false_stmt)):
        sizes = [len(st.accepting_set(c)) for c in (0, 1)]
        print(f"  {name}: |accepting(c=0)| = {sizes[0]}, "
              f"|accepting(c=1)| = {sizes[1]}   (|G| = 12)")

    # accepting set == range of simulator, for the false statement too
    for st, name in ((true_stmt, "true"), (false_stmt, "false")):
        for c in (0, 1):
            assert set(st.accepting_set(c)) == {st.sim(z, c) for z in st.elements()}
    print("accepting set == range of simulator, both statements, both challenges: True")

# 2. Parallel repetition and the cheat set
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cheat_set(
    stmt: AffineStatement,
    commitments: Sequence[int],
    respond: Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], Tuple[int, ...]],
) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Challenge vectors an already-committed prover can answer."""
    n = len(commitments)
    good: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for c in product((0, 1), repeat=n):
        z = respond(c)
        if all(stmt.accepts((commitments[i], c[i], z[i])) for i in range(n)):
            good.append(c)
    return good


def best_cheating_prover(
    stmt: AffineStatement, commitments: Sequence[int]
) -> Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """The optimal (unbounded) adversary: for each challenge vector, answer
    each round with any response that satisfies the verification equation,
    if one exists."""
    n = len(commitments)

    def respond(c: Tuple[int, ...]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
        out: List[int] = []
        for i in range(n):
            found = 0
            for z in stmt.elements():
                if stmt.accepts((commitments[i], c[i], z)):
                    found = z
                    break
            out.append(found)
        return tuple(out)

    return respond


def demo_parallel_repetition() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. PARALLEL REPETITION: EXHAUSTIVE CHEAT-SET ENUMERATION")
    print("=" * 74)

    false_stmt = AffineStatement(12, 4, 1)

    print("false statement 4w = 1: optimal unbounded prover, all commitment")
    print("vectors enumerated; |cheat set| out of 2^n.\n")
    for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        worst = 0
        for commitments in product(range(12), repeat=n):
            cs = cheat_set(false_stmt, commitments, best_cheating_prover(false_stmt, commitments))
            worst = max(worst, len(cs))
        print(f"  n = {n}: max |cheat set| over all commitments = {worst} "
              f"out of {2 ** n}   (bound: 1, fraction <= {1 / 2 ** n:.6f})")

    print("\ntrue statement 4w = 8: honest prover with witness 2, tapes all zero")
    for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):

        def honest(c: Tuple[int, ...], n: int = n) -> Tuple[int, ...]:

# 4. The Fiat-Shamir inversion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def forgery_exists(stmt: AffineStatement, hash_fn: Callable[[int], int]) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Return an accepted non-interactive pair (a, z), or None."""
    for z in stmt.elements():
        for c in (0, 1):
            a = (stmt.f(z) - stmt.chi(c, stmt.target)) % stmt.m
            if hash_fn(a) == c:
                return (a, z)
    return None


def all_hashes(m: int) -> Iterable[Callable[[int], int]]:
    """Enumerate every function Z/m -> {0,1}.  Only feasible for tiny m."""
    for bits in product((0, 1), repeat=m):
        yield (lambda a, bits=bits: bits[a % m])


def demo_fiat_shamir() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. THE FIAT-SHAMIR INVERSION")
    print("=" * 74)

    # small group so that all 2^m hash functions can be enumerated
    true_small = AffineStatement(6, 2, 4)    # 2w = 4 mod 6 : witnesses 2, 5
    false_small = AffineStatement(6, 2, 1)   # 2w = 1 mod 6 : none

    print(f"group Z/6, f(x) = 2x; image = {true_small.image()}")
    print(f"true  statement 2w = 4: witnesses {true_small.witnesses()}")
    print(f"false statement 2w = 1: witnesses {false_small.witnesses()}")

    total = 2 ** 6
    forgeable_true = sum(1 for h in all_hashes(6) if forgery_exists(true_small, h))
    forgeable_false = sum(1 for h in all_hashes(6) if forgery_exists(false_small, h))
    print(f"\nhash functions Z/6 -> {{0,1}} enumerated: {total}")
    print(f"  TRUE  statement: hashes admitting a forgery = {forgeable_true} / {total}")
    print(f"  FALSE statement: hashes admitting a forgery = {forgeable_false} / {total}")
    print(f"  => forgery-free hashes exist iff the statement is FALSE: "
          f"{forgeable_true == total and forgeable_false < total}")

    # the canonical forgery-free hash on the false statement
    image = set(false_small.image())
    image_hash: Callable[[int], int] = lambda a: 1 if a % 6 in image else 0
    print(f"\nimage colouring on the false statement is forgery-free : "
          f"{forgery_exists(false_small, image_hash) is None}")
    print(f"image colouring on the true  statement is forgeable     : "
          f"{forgery_exists(true_small, image_hash) is not None}")

# 5. The linear protocol over F_q
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


class LinearStatement:
    """f(x) = k*x on F_q (q prime), target T; challenges range over F_q."""

    def __init__(self, q: int, k: int, target: int) -> None:
        self.q: int = q
        self.k: int = k % q
        self.target: int = target % q

    def f(self, x: int) -> int:
        return (self.k * x) % self.q

    def elements(self) -> List[int]:
        return list(range(self.q))

    def witnesses(self) -> List[int]:
        return [w for w in self.elements() if self.f(w) == self.target]

    def accepts(self, a: int, c: int, z: int) -> bool:
        return self.f(z) == (a + c * self.target) % self.q

    def real(self, w: int, r: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return (self.f(r), c, (r + c * w) % self.q)

    def sim(self, z: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return ((self.f(z) - c * self.target) % self.q, c, z)

    def extract(self, c: int, z: int, c2: int, z2: int) -> int:
        """w = (c - c')^{-1} (z - z') in F_q."""
        diff = (c - c2) % self.q
        inv = pow(diff, self.q - 2, self.q)  # Fermat inverse, q prime
        return (inv * (z - z2)) % self.q


def demo_linear() -> None:
    print()

    print("5. LINEAR PROTOCOL OVER F_q: SOUNDNESS q^{-n} AND LINEAR EXTRACTION")
    print("=" * 74)

    zero_stmt = LinearStatement(q, 0, 1)   # no witness

    print(f"F_5, identity map, target 3 : witnesses {id_stmt.witnesses()}")
    print(f"F_5, zero map,     target 1 : witnesses {zero_stmt.witnesses()}")

    # perfect zero knowledge over every challenge in F_q
    ok = all(
        Counter(id_stmt.real(3, r, c) for r in id_stmt.elements())
        == Counter(id_stmt.sim(z, c) for z in id_stmt.elements())
        for c in range(q)
    )
    print(f"perfect zero knowledge for every challenge in F_5 : {ok}")

    # linear extraction from two distinct challenges
    r = 4
    a = id_stmt.f(r)
    c, c2 = 1, 4
    z = (r + c * 3) % q
    z2 = (r + c2 * 3) % q
    assert id_stmt.accepts(a, c, z) and id_stmt.accepts(a, c2, z2)
    print(f"extraction from challenges {c} and {c2}: "
          f"(c-c')^-1 (z-z') = {id_stmt.extract(c, z, c2, z2)}  (witness is 3)")

    print("\nfalse statement, optimal unbounded prover, all commitments:")

            for cs in product(range(q), repeat=n):
                answerable = True
                for i in range(n):
                    if not any(zero_stmt.accepts(commitments[i], cs[i], z)
                               for z in zero_stmt.elements()):
                        answerable = False
                        break
                good += 1 if answerable else 0
            worst = max(worst, good)
        print(f"  n = {n}: max |cheat set| = {worst} out of {q ** n} "
              f"(bound 1, fraction <= {1 / q ** n:.6f})")

# 6. OR-composition
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def or_left(
    s1: AffineStatement, s2: AffineStatement, w1: int, c: int, r: int, z: int, d: int
) -> OrTranscript:
    m = s1.m
    return (
        s1.f(r),
        (s2.f(z) - s2.chi(d, s2.target)) % m,
        c ^ d,
        d,
        (r + s1.chi(c ^ d, w1)) % m,
        z,
    )


def or_right(
    s1: AffineStatement, s2: AffineStatement, w2: int, c: int, r: int, z: int, d: int
) -> OrTranscript:
    m = s1.m
    return (
        (s1.f(z) - s1.chi(d, s1.target)) % m,
        s2.f(r),
        d,
        c ^ d,
        z,
        (r + s2.chi(c ^ d, w2)) % m,
    )


def or_accepts(s1: AffineStatement, s2: AffineStatement, c: int, t: OrTranscript) -> bool:
    a1, a2, c1, c2, z1, z2 = t
    return (c1 ^ c2) == c and s1.accepts((a1, c1, z1)) and s2.accepts((a2, c2, z2))


def demo_or_composition() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. OR-COMPOSITION: WHICH-THEOREM HIDING")
    print("=" * 74)

    s1 = AffineStatement(6, 2, 4)   # witnesses 2, 5
    s2 = AffineStatement(6, 3, 3)   # witnesses 1, 3, 5
    w1, w2 = s1.witnesses()[0], s2.witnesses()[0]
    print(f"s1: 2w = 4 mod 6, witnesses {s1.witnesses()} (using {w1})")
    print(f"s2: 3w = 3 mod 6, witnesses {s2.witnesses()} (using {w2})")

    rand = [(r, z, d) for r in range(6) for z in range(6) for d in (0, 1)]
    for c in (0, 1):
        left = Counter(or_left(s1, s2, w1, c, r, z, d) for (r, z, d) in rand)
        right = Counter(or_right(s1, s2, w2, c, r, z, d) for (r, z, d) in rand)
        complete = all(or_accepts(s1, s2, c, t) for t in left)
        print(f"challenge {c}: left view == right view : {left == right}   "
              f"(all accepted: {complete}, {sum(left.values())} conversations)")

    print("\nThe verifier cannot tell which of the two statements the prover")
    print("is able to prove: the two strategies induce the same distribution.")

    # disjunctive soundness, illustrated
    r, z, d = 1, 2, 0
    t0 = or_left(s1, s2, w1, 0, r, z, d)
    t1 = or_left(s1, s2, w1, 1, r, z, d)
    shares = (t0[0], t0[1]) == (t1[0], t1[1])
    print(f"\ntwo conversations, same commitments {shares}, challenges 0 and 1")
    print(f"  => sub-challenges differ somewhere: "
          f"{(t0[2] != t1[2]) or (t0[3] != t1[3])} => a witness is extractable")

    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. A TOY PROVABILITY COMPILER")
    print("=" * 74)

    # Formal system: "proofs" are strings; a proof checks the theorem

    # both to witnesses of the public statement 4w = 8 mod 12.
    checking_proofs: Dict[str, int] = {"short derivation": 2, "long derivation": 5}
    stmt = AffineStatement(12, 4, 8)

    print("theorem THM has two checking proofs, encoded as group elements:")
    for p, e in checking_proofs.items():
        print(f"  {p!r:20s} -> {e:2d}   is a witness: {stmt.f(e) == stmt.target}")

    print("\n(i) identical views for the two proofs, each challenge:")
    for c in (0, 1):
        v = [stmt.real_view(e, c) for e in checking_proofs.values()]
        print(f"  challenge {c}: views equal = {v[0] == v[1]}, "

    print("\n(ii) conviction: a double answer certifies provability.")
    r = 3
    a = stmt.f(r)
    z0, z1 = r, (r + 2) % 12
    w = AffineStatement.extract(z0, z1, 12)
    provable = stmt.f(w) == stmt.target
    print(f"  extracted {w}; statement true => THM provable : {provable}")

    print("\n(iii) an UNPROVABLE theorem compiles to 4w = 1, which has no")
    print("      witness; over n rounds a committed prover survives with")
    print("      probability at most 2^-n:")
    unprov = AffineStatement(12, 4, 1)
    for n in (1, 4, 10, 128):
        print(f"      n = {n:3d}: bound = 2^-{n} = {2.0 ** (-n):.3e}")
    print(f"      witnesses of the compiled statement: {unprov.witnesses()}")

    print("\n(iv) BOUNDARY: with the zero homomorphism every element is a")
    print("     witness, so the compilation certifies nothing at all.")
    vacuous = AffineStatement(12, 0, 0)
    print(f"     f = 0, target 0: |witnesses| = {len(vacuous.witnesses())} "
          f"= |G| = 12  -> vacuous")

def field_inverse(x: int, q: int) -> int:
    """Inverse in F_q for prime q, by Fermat's little theorem: x^(q-2)."""
    if x % q == 0:
        raise ZeroDivisionError("no inverse of 0 in F_q")
    return pow(x % q, q - 2, q)


def accepts(k: int, target: int, q: int, a: int, c: int, z: int) -> bool:
    """Verification equation f(z) = a + c * target with f(x) = k*x on F_q."""
    return (k * z) % q == (a + c * target) % q


def extract_witness(
    k: int, target: int, q: int, a: int, c1: int, z1: int, c2: int, z2: int
) -> int:
    """Return w with k*w = target, from two accepted answers at commitment a.

    Preconditions: c1 != c2 and both transcripts are accepted.
    Correctness: subtracting the two verification equations gives
        k*(z1 - z2) = (c1 - c2)*target,
    so w = (c1 - c2)^{-1} * (z1 - z2) satisfies k*w = target.
    Cost: O(log q) for the modular inverse, O(1) field operations otherwise.
    """
    if c1 % q == c2 % q:
        raise ValueError("challenges must be distinct")
    if not accepts(k, target, q, a, c1, z1):
        raise ValueError("first transcript is not accepted")
    if not accepts(k, target, q, a, c2, z2):
        raise ValueError("second transcript is not accepted")
    inv = field_inverse((c1 - c2) % q, q)
    return (inv * (z1 - z2)) % q


def extract_witness_boolean(z_false: int, z_true: int, modulus: int) -> int:
    """Boolean special case (q = 2 style challenges 0 and 1) in Z/m:
    the linear solve degenerates to a subtraction."""
    return (z_true - z_false) % modulus

def answerable(k: int, target: int, q: int, a: int, c: int) -> bool:
    """Is there any z in F_q with k*z = a + c*target?  (Unbounded prover.)"""
    return any((k * z) % q == (a + c * target) % q for z in range(q))


def cheat_set(
    k: int, target: int, q: int, commitments: Sequence[int]

    """All challenge vectors the optimal unbounded prover can answer.

    commitments are fixed, the optimum is round-wise: a vector is answerable
    iff every coordinate is.  Cost: O(q^n * n * q) checks, or O(n*q^2) if the

        for i in range(n)

        tuple(c)
        for c in product(range(q), repeat=n)
        if all(table[i][c[i]] for i in range(n))
    }

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, List, Optional, Tuple


def hom(k: int, m: int, x: int) -> int:
    return (k * x) % m


def chi(c: int, x: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Boolean challenge selector: chi(0, x) = 0, chi(1, x) = x."""
    return x % m if c == 1 else 0


def find_forgery(
    k: int, target: int, m: int, hash_fn: Callable[[int], int]
) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Search for an accepted non-interactive pair (a, z).

    By the fixed-point description, such a pair exists iff for some response z
    and some challenge bit c one has Hash(f(z) - chi(c, T)) = c.  Scanning all
    z and both bits costs O(|G|) hash evaluations.
    """
    for z in range(m):
        for c in (0, 1):
            a = (hom(k, m, z) - chi(c, target, m)) % m
            if hash_fn(a) == c:
                return (a, z)
    return None


def image_of(k: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    return sorted({hom(k, m, x) for x in range(m)})


def image_hash(k: int, m: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """The canonical candidate: 1 on the image of f, 0 elsewhere.

    Cost: O(|G|) to tabulate the image, O(1) per evaluation.
    """
    image = set(image_of(k, m))
    return lambda a: 1 if a % m in image else 0


def build_forgery_free_hash(
    k: int, target: int, m: int
) -> Optional[Callable[[int], int]]:
    """Return a forgery-free hash if one exists, else None.

    The statement has a witness iff target lies in the image of f; in that case
    NO hash is forgery-free and None is returned.  Otherwise the image
    colouring works, and is returned.  Cost: O(|G|).
    """
    if target % m in set(image_of(k, m)):
        return None
    return image_hash(k, m)

        else:
            forgery = find_forgery(k, target, m, h)
            print(f"{label}: image colouring is forgery-free = {forgery is None}")

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

Transcript = Tuple[int, int, int]


def hom(k: int, m: int, x: int) -> int:
    return (k * x) % m


def chi(c: int, x: int, m: int) -> int:
    return x % m if c == 1 else 0


def real_view(k: int, target: int, m: int, w: int, c: int) -> Counter:
    """Multiset of honest transcripts as the tape runs over the whole group."""
    return Counter((hom(k, m, r), c, (r + chi(c, w, m)) % m) for r in range(m))


def sim_view(k: int, target: int, m: int, c: int) -> Counter:
    """Multiset of simulated transcripts, computed without any witness."""
    return Counter(
        ((hom(k, m, z) - chi(c, target, m)) % m, c, z) for z in range(m)
    )


def accepting_set(k: int, target: int, m: int, c: int) -> List[Transcript]:
    """All transcripts with challenge c satisfying the verification equation.
    Cost: O(|G|^2) pairs tested, O(|G|) survive."""
    return [
        (a, c, z)
        for a in range(m)
        for z in range(m)
        if hom(k, m, z) == (a + chi(c, target, m)) % m
    ]


def certify(k: int, target: int, m: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Certify, for both challenges: (i) real view = simulated view for every
    witness; (ii) accepting set = range of the simulator; (iii) the accepting
    set has exactly |G| elements, whether or not a witness exists."""
    witnesses = [w for w in range(m) if hom(k, m, w) == target % m]
    report: Dict[str, object] = {
        "group_order": m,
        "witnesses": witnesses,
        "kernel_size": sum(1 for x in range(m) if hom(k, m, x) == 0),
    }
    for c in (0, 1):
        sv = sim_view(k, target, m, c)
        report[f"pzk_challenge_{c}"] = all(
            real_view(k, target, m, w, c) == sv for w in witnesses
        )
        acc = accepting_set(k, target, m, c)
        report[f"accepting_size_challenge_{c}"] = len(acc)
        report[f"accepting_is_sim_range_challenge_{c}"] = set(acc) == set(sv)
    return report

def worst_case_cheat_size(k: int, target: int, q: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Brute force over all commitment vectors and all challenge vectors."""
    worst = 0
    for commitments in product(range(q), repeat=n):
        table = [[answerable(k, target, q, commitments[i], c) for c in range(q)]

        <span><span class="swatch" style="background:#f2c14e"></span>this conversation</span>
        <span><span class="swatch" style="background:#141b23;border:1px solid #232e3a"></span>rejected</span>
      </div>
      <div id="gridWrap"></div>
      <div class="note" id="gridNote"></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="panel">
  <h2>3 · Zero knowledge: the honest prover versus the simulator</h2>
  <p class="note">The simulator holds no witness at all. It picks a response
  <span class="mono">z</span> uniformly and back-computes the commitment
  <span class="mono">a = f(z) − c·T</span>. If the two lists below match as
  multisets, the verifier’s view contains literally nothing that a
  witness-free machine could not have written by itself.</p>
  <div class="row">
    <div class="col"><div id="viewCmp"></div></div>
    <div class="col"><div id="viewTable"></div></div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="panel">
  <h2>4 · Extraction, and why the verifier believes anything at all</h2>
  <p class="note">Answering <em>both</em> challenges at one commitment hands the
  witness over: subtract the two responses.</p>
  <div id="extract"></div>
</div>

<div class="panel">
  <h2>5 · Amplification: the exponential gap</h2>
  <div class="ctl"><label>number of parallel rounds n = <span id="nlab" class="mono">4</span></label>
    <input type="range" id="n" min="1" max="40" value="4"></div>
  <div id="amp"></div>
</div>

</div>
<script>
(function(){
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const state = {m:12,k:4,t:8,r:0,w:2,c:0,n:4};

  function fill(sel, values, cur){
    sel.innerHTML = values.map(v=>`<option value="${v}" ${v===cur?"selected":""}>${v}</option>`).join("");
  }
  function hom(x){ return ((state.k*x)%state.m+state.m)%state.m; }
  function chi(c,x){ return c===1 ? ((x%state.m)+state.m)%state.m : 0; }
  function accepts(a,c,z){ return hom(z) === (((a+chi(c,state.t))%state.m)+state.m)%state.m; }
  function witnesses(){ const o=[]; for(let x=0;x<state.m;x++) if(hom(x)===state.t%state.m) o.push(x); return o; }
  function kernel(){ const o=[]; for(let x=0;x<state.m;x++) if(hom(x)===0) o.push(x); return o; }
  function image(){ const s=new Set(); for(let x=0;x<state.m;x++) s.add(hom(x)); return [...s].sort((a,b)=>a-b); }
  function gcd(a,b){ return b?gcd(b,a%b):a; }

  function rebuildSelectors(){
    fill($("m"), [4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12,15,16], state.m);
    fill($("k"), Array.from({length:state.m},(_,i)=>i), state.k);
    fill($("t"), Array.from({length:state.m},(_,i)=>i), state.t);
    fill($("r"), Array.from({length:state.m},(_,i)=>i), state.r);
    const ws = witnesses();
    $("w").innerHTML = ws.length
      ? ws.map(v=>`<option value="${v}" ${v===state.w?"selected":""}>${v}</option>`).join("")
      : `<option value="-1">— no witness exists —</option>`;
    if(ws.length && !ws.includes(state.w)){ state.w = ws[0]; $("w").value = ws[0]; }
    if(!ws.length) state.w = -1;
  }

  function renderStatement(){
    const ws = witnesses(), ker = kernel(), im = image();
    const isTrue = ws.length>0;
    $("statementInfo").innerHTML = `
      <div class="eq">claim:  ∃ w ∈ ℤ/${state.m} :  ${state.k}·w ≡ ${state.t}  (mod ${state.m})</div>
      <p><span class="pill ${isTrue?'good':'bad'}">${isTrue?'TRUE':'FALSE'}</span>
      <span class="pill">image of f = {${im.join(", ")}}</span></p>
      <p><b>witnesses</b> (${ws.length}): <span class="mono">${ws.length?ws.join(", "):"none"}</span><br>
         <b>kernel of f</b> (${ker.length}): <span class="mono">${ker.join(", ")}</span></p>
      <p class="note">The witness set is always a coset of the kernel, so
      <span class="mono">|witnesses| = |ker f|</span> whenever a witness exists —
      here ${isTrue? ws.length+" = "+ker.length : "vacuously, since there is none"}.
      When <span class="mono">gcd(k,m) = 1</span> the map is injective, the kernel is
      trivial and the witness is <em>unique</em> — yet the privacy below is
      unchanged. Privacy is not made of witness ambiguity.</p>`;
  }

  function renderConversation(){
    const w = state.w>=0 ? state.w : 0;
    const a = hom(state.r), z = ((state.r + chi(state.c,w))%state.m+state.m)%state.m;
    const ok = accepts(a,state.c,z);
    const hasW = state.w>=0;
    $("convo").innerHTML = `
      <div class="eq">move 1 — commit:   a = f(r) = ${state.k}·${state.r} = <b>${a}</b></div>
      <div class="eq">move 2 — challenge: c = <b>${state.c}</b></div>
      <div class="eq">move 3 — respond:  z = r ${state.c?("+ w = "+state.r+" + "+w):""} = <b>${z}</b></div>
      <div class="eq">verify:  f(z) = ${hom(z)} ${ok?"=":"≠"} a + c·T = ${((a+chi(state.c,state.t))%state.m+state.m)%state.m}</div>
      <p class="verdict ${ok?'ok':'no'}">${ok?"ACCEPTED":"REJECTED"}${hasW?"":" — no witness exists, so the prover is guessing"}</p>`;
    return {a,z};
  }

  function renderGrid(hit){
    const m = state.m, c = state.c;
    let html = `<div class="grid" style="grid-template-columns:repeat(${m},1fr)">`;
    let count = 0;
    for(let z=m-1;z>=0;z--){
      for(let a=0;a<m;a++){
        const acc = accepts(a,c,z);
        if(acc) count++;
        const isHit = hit && hit.a===a && hit.z===z;
        html += `<div class="cell ${acc?"acc":""} ${isHit?"hit":""}" title="a=${a}, z=${z}">${acc?"✓":""}</div>`;
      }
    }
    html += `</div>`;
    $("gridWrap").innerHTML = html;
    $("gridNote").innerHTML =
      `Rows are responses <span class="mono">z</span> (top = ${m-1}), columns are
       commitments <span class="mono">a</span>. Accepting cells:
       <b class="mono">${count}</b> = |G| = ${m}. Change the target to a value that
       makes the statement false: the count does <em>not</em> move. The accepting
       set is exactly the graph of the simulator, so its size is a constant of the
       group — it cannot leak whether the claim is true.`;
  }

  function multiset(list){
    const map = new Map();
    list.forEach(k=>map.set(k,(map.get(k)||0)+1));
    return map;
  }
  function sameMultiset(A,B){
    if(A.size!==B.size) return false;
    for(const [k,v] of A) if(B.get(k)!==v) return false;
    return true;
  }

  function renderViews(){
    const ws = witnesses();
    if(!ws.length){
      $("viewCmp").innerHTML = `<p class="note">The statement is false, so there is no
        honest prover to compare with. (The simulator still produces perfectly
        accepted conversations — which is exactly why a single transcript proves
        nothing.)</p>`;
      $("viewTable").innerHTML = "";
      return;
    }
    const c = state.c;
    const real = [], sim = [];
    for(let r=0;r<state.m;r++) real.push(`(${hom(r)}, ${c}, ${((r+chi(c,state.w))%state.m+state.m)%state.m})`);
    for(let z=0;z<state.m;z++) sim.push(`(${((hom(z)-chi(c,state.t))%state.m+state.m)%state.m}, ${c}, ${z})`);
    const equal = sameMultiset(multiset(real),multiset(sim));

    let cross = "";
    if(ws.length>1){
      const other = ws.find(x=>x!==state.w);
      const realOther = [];
      for(let r=0;r<state.m;r++) realOther.push(`(${hom(r)}, ${c}, ${((r+chi(c,other))%state.m+state.m)%state.m})`);
      const eq2 = sameMultiset(multiset(real),multiset(realOther));
      cross = `<p class="verdict ${eq2?'ok':'no'}">witness ${state.w} vs witness ${other}:
               views ${eq2?"identical":"different"}</p>`;
    }

    $("viewCmp").innerHTML = `
      <p class="bigstat verdict ${equal?'ok':'no'}">${equal?"views are identical":"views differ"}</p>
      <p class="note">Honest execution with witness <span class="mono">${state.w}</span>,
      challenge <span class="mono">${c}</span>, versus the witness-free simulator.
      Both are multisets of ${state.m} conversations.</p>
      ${cross}
      <p class="note">Two provers holding different proofs of the same fact are
      therefore indistinguishable to the verifier — the punchline for
      zero-knowledge proofs of provability.</p>`;

    const rows = real.map((v,i)=>`<tr><td class="mono">${v}</td><td class="mono">${sim[i]}</td></tr>`).join("");
    $("viewTable").innerHTML = `<table><thead><tr>
        <th>honest, tape r = 0…${state.m-1}</th><th>simulated, response z = 0…${state.m-1}</th>
      </tr></thead><tbody>${rows}</tbody></table>
      <p class="note">The lists are not equal <em>row by row</em> — they are equal as
      multisets, re-indexed by the bijection r ↦ r + c·w of the tape space. That
      bijection is the entire mechanism of privacy.</p>`;
  }

  function renderExtract(){
    const ws = witnesses();
    const a = hom(state.r);
    if(!ws.length){
      $("extract").innerHTML = `<p class="note">The statement is false. A committed
        prover can answer at most <em>one</em> of the two challenges at any
        commitment — if it could answer both, subtraction would produce a witness,
        and none exists. Concretely, at a = ${a} the two answers cannot both be
        given.</p>`;
      return;
    }
    const z0 = state.r, z1 = ((state.r+state.w)%state.m+state.m)%state.m;
    const ext = ((z1-z0)%state.m+state.m)%state.m;
    $("extract").innerHTML = `
      <div class="eq">commitment a = f(${state.r}) = ${a}</div>
      <div class="eq">answer to c = 0:  z₀ = ${z0}     (checks: f(z₀) = ${hom(z0)} = a ✓)</div>
      <div class="eq">answer to c = 1:  z₁ = ${z1}     (checks: f(z₁) = ${hom(z1)} = a + T = ${((a+state.t)%state.m+state.m)%state.m} ✓)</div>
      <div class="eq">extracted witness: z₁ − z₀ = <b>${ext}</b>,  and f(${ext}) = ${hom(ext)} = T ${hom(ext)===state.t%state.m?"✓":"✗"}</div>
      <p class="note">Note what this costs the prover: nothing, as long as she never
      gives both answers at the same commitment. The verifier picks one challenge
      per commitment, so extraction is a thought experiment — but the fact that it
      <em>would</em> work is precisely why a cheat cannot survive many rounds.</p>`;
  }

  function renderAmp(){
    const n = state.n;
    const hasW = witnesses().length>0;
    const bound = Math.pow(2,-n);
    $("nlab").textContent = n;
    $("amp").innerHTML = `
      <div class="row">
        <div class="col">
          <p><span class="pill">challenge vectors: 2<sup>${n}</sup> = ${Math.pow(2,n).toLocaleString()}</span></p>
          <p>without a witness, a committed prover answers <span class="bigstat">at most 1</span>
             of them — an accepting fraction of at most
             <span class="mono">${bound.toExponential(3)}</span>.</p>
          <p>with a witness, an honest prover answers
             <span class="bigstat">all ${Math.pow(2,n).toLocaleString()}</span>.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="col">
          <p class="note">This statement is currently
             <span class="pill ${hasW?'good':'bad'}">${hasW?'TRUE':'FALSE'}</span>, so the
             ${hasW?"second":"first"} line applies. There is no behaviour in between:
             the accepting fraction is either ≤ 2<sup>−n</sup> or exactly 1.</p>
          <p class="note">Replace the coin by a challenge drawn from a field with q
             elements and the same argument gives q<sup>−n</sup>, with extraction
             becoming the linear solve w = (c − c′)<sup>−1</sup>(z − z′).</p>
        </div>
      </div>`;
  }

  function renderAll(){
    renderStatement();
    const conv = renderConversation();
    renderGrid(conv);
    renderViews();
    renderExtract();
    renderAmp();
  }

  function bind(){
    $("m").onchange = e=>{ state.m=+e.target.value;
      state.k=Math.min(state.k,state.m-1); state.t=Math.min(state.t,state.m-1);
      state.r=Math.min(state.r,state.m-1); rebuildSelectors(); renderAll(); };
    $("k").onchange = e=>{ state.k=+e.target.value; rebuildSelectors(); renderAll(); };
    $("t").onchange = e=>{ state.t=+e.target.value; rebuildSelectors(); renderAll(); };
    $("r").onchange = e=>{ state.r=+e.target.value; renderAll(); };
    $("w").onchange = e=>{ state.w=+e.target.value; renderAll(); };
    $("c").onchange = e=>{ state.c=+e.target.value; renderAll(); };
    $("n").oninput  = e=>{ state.n=+e.target.value; renderAmp(); };
    $("btnTrue").onclick = ()=>{ state.m=12; state.k=4; state.t=8; state.r=3;
      rebuildSelectors(); state.w=witnesses()[0]; rebuildSelectors(); renderAll(); };
    $("btnFalse").onclick = ()=>{ state.m=12; state.k=4; state.t=1; state.r=3;
      rebuildSelectors(); renderAll(); };
    $("btnInj").onclick = ()=>{ state.m=12; state.k=5; state.t=7; state.r=3;
      rebuildSelectors(); state.w=witnesses()[0]; rebuildSelectors(); renderAll(); };
  }

  rebuildSelectors(); bind(); renderAll();
})();
</script>
</body>
</html>
